newsitem.title: FRANCE: Rexrodt sees gold revaluation this year.
newsitem.headline: Rexrodt sees gold revaluation this year.

text.p: German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said on Monday his country could and should proceed with plans to revalue gold reserves this year if the Bundesbank agreed -- as feuding over how to fill the gap in Germany's budget continued.

Some market participants have raised concerns that the measure, announced earlier this month, was a "fudge" to enable Germany to meet the criteria for European economic and monetary union (EMU) laid down in the Maastricht Treaty.

Asked whether the plan to revalue Germany's gold reserves could take place in 1997 or 1998, Rexrodt, speaking at the annual OECD ministerial meeting, said: "It is possible this year, but that depends on an assessment from the Bundesbank."
"My opinion is that we can proceed and we should proceed," he told a news conference. "There is space for such a revaluation and it is a serious measure."

Rexrodt said the proceeds from the gold revaluation would effect Germany's debt position if they were put into the unity fund, which is used to fund the cost of German reunification. "It would then impact Germany's general debt position," he said.

German unemployment, which peaked in January at a 64-year record of 4.7 million, has blown away Bonn's budget projections. And recent tax projections revealed a new gap of nearly 20 billion marks ($11.9 billion) in revenues this year.

Rexrodt earlier refuted claims made by German Finance Minister Theo Waigel that other government departments had botched economic forecasts and left Waigel searching for billions of marks to cut Bonn's deficit to meet the EMU convergence criteria for European monetary union.
He said responsibility for the forecasts was shared widely.
"The economic estimates are the result of common work of the different ministries and not only of the economics ministry," Rexrodt told reporters.

Government feuding has broken out into the open after Waigel refused to rule out tax hikes to cut the budget deficit to the limit of three percent of gross domestic product required to join EMU's starting line-up in 1999.
Rexrodt's Free Democrat party (FDP), junior partners in Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition, passed a resolution on Sunday rejecting tax increases to plug the budget holes.

Rexrodt said on Monday he could imagine Bonn taking further steps towards privatising Deutsche Telekom this year, although he did not give any further details of a possible further sale from Bonn's remaining 74 percent stake.
"I could imagine that we agree further steps towards privatising Deutsche Telekom this year to a strategic investor," Rexrodt said.
The government floated 26 percent of Deutsche Telekom last November in an issue which raised 20 billion marks.
Waigel said earlier this month Bonn was considering an early sale of additional shares in Telekom later this year but said it would not help Germany's EMU hopes.

Instead, Waigel said the proceeds of his plan, which has drawn criticism since Bonn is obliged under law not to sell any more shares on stock exchanges before the year 2000, would be used to pay off old debt. ($ = 1.685 German Marks)
